title: The Million Tiny Files

scenario.situation: A streaming pipeline writes one file per sensor event to the data lake. Over the past month, query latency on the lake has climbed from 4 seconds to 90 seconds. The lead wants to scale up the query cluster.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The lead is convinced the query cluster is undersized — the data volume has tripled and the nodes must be saturated.
scenario.question: Is the cluster actually the bottleneck, or is something else throttling query performance?

decisions.prompt: The lead wants you to justify a cluster upgrade. How do you frame your investigation?

options.label: Benchmark the cluster under load
options.detail: Run heavy queries and watch CPU and memory utilization to see if nodes are saturated.
options.consequence: CPU and memory look high during queries — but high resource use during a slow query doesn't mean the cluster is too small. It might just mean the query itself is doing something pathological. You've confirmed the symptom, not the cause.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the lead's hypothesis and mistook a symptom for a root cause.

options.label: Diagnostic decomposition of query execution
options.detail: Break a slow query into its phases — planning, file listing, metadata fetch, scan, shuffle — and measure time spent in each phase.
options.consequence: The query plan shows almost all latency sits in the metadata and file-open phases, not in data scanning or shuffling. This points away from cluster size entirely and opens a structural thread worth following.

options.label: Compare performance across query types
options.detail: Run a mix of aggregations, joins, and point lookups to see which are slowest.
options.consequence: All query types are slow, not just complex ones. That's a clue, but without knowing why, you've added data points without a direction. You're still not sure if it's the cluster or something else.
options.divergenceCost: Gathered broad symptoms without a framework to interpret them.

options.label: Scale up the cluster as a test
options.detail: Double the node count and see if latency drops.
options.consequence: Latency barely moves after scaling. The team has spent real money on an experiment that didn't isolate the variable — and the lead is confused rather than convinced.
options.divergenceCost: Treated infrastructure spend as a diagnostic instrument — expensive and inconclusive.

decisions.prompt: Query-phase decomposition shows file-open overhead dominates. Which metric do you examine to confirm the structural problem?

artifact.title: Data lake storage — total size by table (TB)
artifact.caption: sensor_events is the largest table by raw size — but is data volume really the problem?

options.label: Total data volume per table (TB)
options.detail: Compare how many terabytes each table occupies to find the heaviest one.
options.consequence: sensor_events is the biggest table — which seems to confirm the cluster is overwhelmed by data volume. But the aggregated_hourly table holds similar logical content in far fewer files and queries in under 3 seconds. Volume alone doesn't explain the gap.
options.divergenceCost: Measured data size when the bottleneck was file count — the wrong unit entirely.

options.label: File count and median file size per table
options.detail: Count how many physical files exist per table and compute median file size.
options.consequence: The picture is stark: sensor_events holds 14 million files at a median size of 12 KB each. aggregated_hourly holds 900 files averaging 420 MB each — and queries it in seconds. The engine is paying per-file metadata overhead 14 million times per query, not struggling with data volume.

artifact.title: Median file size by table (MB)
artifact.caption: sensor_events median file is 0.012 MB — 35,000× smaller than a right-sized file. 14 million open/close operations per query explain the crawl.

decisions.prompt: File count, not data volume, correlates with the latency spike. What do you tell the lead?

options.label: "It's the small-files problem — skip the upgrade and compact the table."
options.detail: Make the causal call and recommend compaction as the fix.
options.consequence: You may well be right, but you've asserted causation from a correlation without a controlled validation. If something else is also degrading performance, compaction alone won't fully recover latency and your credibility takes a hit.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed causation before a controlled validation — risked credibility on a single correlate.

options.label: "File count is the dominant correlate, not data volume — compaction is the highest-probability fix. Let's run a controlled compaction on one partition and measure latency before we re-architect or spend on compute."
options.detail: Present the finding, acknowledge the causal gap, and propose a low-cost validation step.
options.consequence: The lead sees the evidence clearly, understands why the cluster upgrade hypothesis doesn't hold up, and agrees to a single-partition compaction test. It's cheap, fast, and will confirm or falsify the diagnosis before any major investment.

insight: The cluster wasn't undersized — the query engine was paying a per-file metadata and open overhead across 14 million tiny files, each written by a one-event-per-file streaming pattern. Data volume had tripled but file count had grown far faster, and those are different bottlenecks entirely. The lesson is the small-files problem: in distributed lake engines, file count throttles performance more than data size does, because planning and metadata overhead scales with files, not bytes. Compacting to right-sized files (hundreds of MB) dissolves the bottleneck without touching the cluster.
